description: We're a team of software engineers and computer scientists passionate about space tech. We love bold, unconventional, even "crazy" ideas and want to turn them into real solutions. No specific skill set required, though some software background helps. What we need most is a creative mind, a hardworking attitude, and real passion for the challenge. If you're curious, driven, and ready to build something extraordinary, join us!
summary:
Launch dates slip. At the lunar south pole, a two-week slip can turn a site that sees the Sun and Earth almost the whole mission into one that never sees the Sun at all. We built the Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a browser tool where mission planners drag a "slip slider" and instantly see what a delayed landing costs in power (Sun) and direct-to-Earth communications (Earth). It also shows why, down to the exact ridge doing the blocking.

It compares up to three sites at once, using NASA LRO LOLA terrain, NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides, and a live 3D view of the pole with terrain-aware shadows. Every accuracy number is checked against JPL Horizons and NASA PGDA products. Everything is precomputed, so there is no backend and answers update in milliseconds.

This matters because Artemis and CLPS missions are heading to the pole, where the Sun and Earth hover within a few degrees of the horizon. Tiny terrain details decide whether a lander survives. We turn "the launch slipped three weeks" into "here is the best site and date now, and why" in under a minute.
details:
What it does

You pick up to three sites, a landing date and a mission length. You get sunlit %, Earth-link %, the longest blackouts, slope and time to the next sunset. Then you drag the slip slider (−30 to +90 days). Every metric, timeline and view updates live, with the change from your original date shown. Here is a real example from our demo script. IM-2 Athena landing on 2030-10-04 has 99.9% Sun and Earth coverage. Slip it 14 days and that drops to 0.0%, with no sunlight at all.

The views

- 3D Terrain: the south pole lit by the real Sun position, with shadows that come from the terrain horizons. Site beacons change color as the Sun and Earth come and go. These are real horizon-based shadows, not a graphics trick.

- Surface: a first-person view where you watch the Sun sink behind the actual ridge.

- Horizon panorama: an unrolled 360° skyline with the Sun and Earth tracks.

- Timelines: a faint ghost of the original date sits under each band, so losses are visible.

- Opportunity map: a heatmap of the whole pole for any date window, scored in a Web Worker.

- Validation panel: shows how far to trust the numbers.

How it works

An offline Python pipeline computes hourly Sun and Earth positions for 2026 to 2033 from NASA SPICE kernels. It ray-marches LOLA elevation data into terrain horizon masks for 12 curated sites and a 2 km grid over the pole. A pure TypeScript engine does the rest in the browser. It treats the Sun and Earth as real disks, not points, and it handles Earth parallax per site. We have about 15 MB of static data on Vercel. There is no backend and no runtime API calls.

Verifiable

Python and TypeScript are tested against shared golden vectors. Against JPL Horizons we ran 336 comparisons, with a max error of about 0.00003° (target 0.02°). Against PGDA long-term averages, 10 of 12 sites land within ±5 percentage points. The outliers are listed and explained in the app. We label our assumptions on screen too (observer height, geometric-only comms, 2 km grid is approximate).

Impact

Planners can stress-test schedule slips in seconds instead of rerunning heavy tools site by site. It speaks to the real question: "is my plan still good?"

Tools

Python 3.12, SpiceyPy, NumPy, Numba, uv, pytest, ruff. React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Canvas 2D, SVG, Web Workers, three.js with React Three Fiber and drei, Vitest. Hosted on Vercel, built on GitHub with Claude Code as a AI coding assistant.

Creative Angle

Existing tools give one query or one long-term average at a time. We give date-specific, terrain-aware answers for many sites at once, and a slider that makes a schedule slip feel physical. We chose an unrolled panorama over a fisheye on purpose because at the pole everything collapses into a thin ring.

What we considered

Sun and Earth sit within about 5 degrees of the horizon, so small errors flip results. We kept the 3D display terrain strictly for looks, so every visibility number still comes from the horizon data. We also skipped a backend, because JPL Horizons has no CORS and precomputed data works offline.
